we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern.

Our investigation focuses on the impact of this transition on the magnetic properties, which is examined through analysis of resistivity, specific heat, and muon spin relaxation measurements. The absence of metal-insulator diversity in specific heat measurements, despite varying Bi concentration, supports the hypothesis that the interaction is localized in nature, with a single parameter describing it. The observed temperature dependence of resistivity in the three samples fits a formula incorporating theories on correlated metals and variable-range hopping, while also considering disorder.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, we identify tight lower and upper bounds for the more general leakage metric through the application of single-letter analysis.

A new hierarchical generative model called MrSARP is introduced in this research, specifically designed for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image generation, to produce SAR images at various resolutions simultaneously. The MrSARP model is trained alongside a discriminator that assesses multiple-resolution images together to verify their realism, representing a target at various resolutions. The study demonstrates the applicability of the MrSARP deep generative model in retrieving high-resolution images from lower resolution images of the same target. The cost function of the model is modified to improve its ability to recover input parameters based on multiple-resolution images. The performance of the model is assessed using conventional super-resolution error metrics on simulated data and is compared with conventional up-sampling and image sharpening methods that utilize sparsity.

To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic formula to solve a resulting polynomial formed by combining the two ellipse equations, allowing for handling cases where the quadruplets of intersection points may be squared, squared root, or conjugated. The proposed method has been implemented in C and validated through numerous tests with diverse input ellipses, demonstrating its efficiency for applications involving multiple overlap area calculations in simulations.

We investigated magnetic excitations of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. Beginning with the 120-degree and striped patterns of magnetism, we used the self-consistent random phase approximation to determine magnon frequencies. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the highest identification rate of 97.4% and surpassed the best comparable approach, which reported an identification rate of 94.7%, by significantly reducing the relative error rate.

By applying the stationary distribution of this process, we can calculate a "heat" flow that corresponds to the system's free energy decrease.  Through mathematical derivation, we show that this heat flow is achievable by constructing a control strategy using the Lagrangian multiplier method. Through specific examples, we have validated our findings and clarified their implications in simulated molecular dynamics.

Our research focuses on a specific setup where two infinite plates, made of the same material, are positioned in a vacuum with a gap in between, and we apply a high-level of mechanical stress on one plate. We observed that this setup can transfer energy from the excited plate to the other, which is not excited, through acoustic waves. Our mathematical model shows that this energy transfer occurs rapidly, exponentially. Additionally, our analysis indicates that this energy transfer occurs at specific, unique rates, which depend on the characteristics of the plates, such as material density and the ability of the material to change shape. Interestingly, this setup can also allow energy to flow bi-directionally and periodically, resulting in a stable, constant energy transfer rate by combining two different energy transfer processes.

Our framework enables the creation of complex optical patterns, known as Laguerre modes, which exhibit self-healing properties, through precision adjustment of the driving field. By optimizing this adjustment, the polariton system converges to desired Laguerre mode configurations, characterized by intricate nodal patterns, in response to changes in the driving field's spatial profile. This can be achieved in two ways: either by adjusting external lenses, which affects the driving field's propagation, or by manipulating the system's effective propagation length, which is influenced by the polariton's effective mass and inter-particle interactions. Our research showcases the capabilities of modern semiconductor-based microcavity systems in achieving precise optical manipulation, which has potential applications in fields such as metrology, imaging, data storage, and quantum information processing.

-22b was studied through observations of broadband optical measurements taken by the Kepler space telescope as the planet passed in front of its host sun-like star over multiple years. By analyzing these data, scientists modeled the planet's size, shape, and ragged irregularities by applying a comprehensive mathematical framework that incorporates variables such as dust production, accretion, and the physical properties of the exoplanet. According to the developed model, the planet's radius fluctuates between 8.3 and 10.1 Earth radii, with its size and shape dynamics indicating that the exoplanet is likely spherical in shape. Furthermore, the model suggests that the mass of the planet is approximately 0.39 Jupiter masses and that the dust particles orbiting the planet have an average diameter of 1.0 to 6.7 micrometers. It was also observed that there is a correlation between the planet's maximum size and the amount of dust present, with increased dust corresponding to a larger planet radius, and that the star's properties remain relatively constant over the course of the observations. According to the developed model, the exoplanet loses mass at a rate of 0.15 Earth masses per billion years and is expected to lose its atmosphere and eventually become uninhabitable in about 200 million years.

The Daany developer team strives to incorporate new features, such as support for TensorFlow and PyTorch, to enhance the overall user experience.

influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same.

Our study focuses on examining non-Gaussian influences on Saha's ionization through the application of Tsallis statistics. We addressed this challenge by generalizing the number density with a non-Gaussian distribution based on Fermi-Dirac theory and then utilising a perturbation method to analyse a simple astrophysical scenario, specifically non-Gaussian temperature effects on hydrogen's $n = 1 \to n' = 2$ transition. We investigated the impact of non-Gaussian influences on a hydrogen atom situated in a 3D Maxwell-Boltzmann electron gas, within a zero boundary condition, by utilising a numerical approach. We analysed and presented numerical outcomes for a variety of parameters, including q-T values, hydrogen atom depth potential and electron gas temperature. These findings illustrate how non-Gaussian influences can alter the conventional helioseismic signs associated with the heliogravitational mixing length parameter.

Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among the models, with notably large adaptable PIC regions required within the MHD domain to achieve such convergence.

a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.
